title: VQ35HR Oil Consumption
issues: Oil consumption is a well-documented issue for the VQ35DE 'Rev-Up' engine (2005-2007 G35), NOT the VQ35HR used in the 2008-2012 EX35
Forum owners of VQ35HR engines consistently report oil consumption is minimal/nonexistent
NHTSA complaints for EX35 are dominated by airbags and steering, not engine oil consumption
Infiniti's oil consumption TSB (ITB08-xxxx) applies to VQ35DE Rev-Up, not VQ35HR
Claim about 'piston ring coking' and 'valve stem seals' as common HR failure modes is not supported by documented evidence specific to EX35
Repair cost ceiling of $2500 likely understates piston ring/engine R&R work, which typically runs $5K-$10K per forum reports
evidence: The VQ35HR engine in the EX35 is widely reported by owners on G35Driver and BobIsTheOilGuy forums to NOT suffer significant oil consumption, with the issue instead being characteristic of the earlier VQ35DE 'Rev-Up' engine that prompted Infiniti TSB ITB08-002d. NHTSA complaint data for the EX35 shows airbags and steering as the dominant issues, with no notable pattern of oil consumption claims specific to this vehicle.

title: Steering Wheel Lock Malfunction
issues: Year range is largely incorrect: the ESCL/electronic steering column lock failure is documented primarily on 2009-2013 G37 and the V36 G35 sedan (2007-2008 with push-button start), not the 2003-2006 V35 G35 which used a conventional key ignition cylinder

Description conflates two different issues: pre-2007 G35s have mechanical ignition/steering lock cylinder problems, while the 'electronic steering lock actuator motor' failure is an ESCL issue affecting 2007+ push-button start models
Repair cost range ($300-$900) is low; documented owner repairs for ESCL replacement typically run $700-$1300+, with dealer parts alone around $500-$1100
DTC codes listed as 'none' but ESCL failures commonly trigger codes such as B2014/B2607 with a yellow KEY warning indicator
evidence: Multiple sources (MyG37 TSB thread, nissanproblems.com, Infiniti of Beachwood, Go-Parts) confirm the ESCL failure as a widespread issue specifically on 2009-2013 Infiniti G37/G25 and related push-button-start models, with Nissan issuing a warranty extension/service campaign on Nissan-branded vehicles but not Infiniti. The 2003-2006 G35 used a traditional ignition key cylinder and does not have the described electronic steering lock actuator motor.

title: Oil Gallery Gasket Leak
issues: Incorrect location: gaskets are on the rear timing cover, not between upper and lower oil pans
Incorrect failure mode: causes internal oil pressure loss leading to catastrophic engine damage, not external leaks onto exhaust/fire hazard
Missing DTC codes: P0011 and P0021 are the classic codes for this failure, entry says 'none'
Repair cost underestimated: realistic range is $950-$2100+, with some quotes reaching $4000, not $400-$1200
Severity rating of 'high' is correct but for the wrong reason (engine failure risk, not fire hazard)
evidence: The VQ37VHR oil gallery gasket failure is a well-documented, infamous issue for 2008-2013 G37s where paper gaskets on the rear timing cover deteriorate, causing internal oil pressure loss, P0011/P0021 codes, VTC rattle, and risk of catastrophic engine failure. Nissan switched to updated metal-reinforced composite gaskets around the 2012-2013 model year, and typical repair costs run $950-$2100, well above the entry's stated range.

title: CVT Judder at Low Speed (2.0T Models)
issues: The Infiniti Q50 does not have a CVT transmission - it uses a 7-speed automatic (RE7R01A/JR710E/JR711E) across all trims including the 2.0T
The described CVT judder issue (belt slip, P17F0/P17F1 codes) is a documented problem on the Infiniti QX60/JX35 and Nissan Pathfinder, NOT the Q50
DTC codes field is empty - the real CVT judder issue has well-known associated codes (P17F0/P17F1) but these don't apply to the Q50 anyway
Description references 'CVT belt and pulleys' which is mechanically inapplicable to the Q50's 7-speed automatic transmission
The 2.0T Q50 (introduced for 2016 model year) specifically pairs the Mercedes-sourced engine with the 7-speed auto, not a CVT
evidence: Multiple Infiniti Q50 forum sources and parts catalogs confirm the Q50 has never been equipped with a CVT - all trims use a 7-speed automatic transmission. The CVT judder/shudder issue with P17F0/P17F1 codes documented in NHTSA TSBs and class-action lawsuits (Batista v. Nissan) applies to the QX60, JX35, and Nissan Pathfinder with the JATCO CVT8HT, not the Q50.

title: Direct Adaptive Steering (Steer-by-Wire) Issues
issues: Year range incorrect: DAS was dropped from Q50 starting the 2022 model year, so 2022-2026 Q50s do not have DAS
Trim description misleading: DAS was tied to ProActive/Deluxe Technology packages across trims (including Premium), not exclusive to Sport/Red Sport; many Sport/Red Sport cars did not have DAS
DTC codes listed as 'none' but real DAS faults produce documented codes (e.g., C13D5-00, C1B90-00, C13E9-00, C13EB-00)
Severity likely understated: NHTSA Recall 16V430000 was issued for DAS malfunctions affecting steering responsiveness — a safety-critical issue, not just 'medium'

Repair cost range ($100-$800) is too low for out-of-warranty DAS hardware failures; DAS uses 3 redundant ECUs and module replacement/programming typically far exceeds $800 (recall reprogramming itself was free)
evidence: DAS is a heavily documented Q50 issue (NHTSA recall 16V430000 from June 2016, numerous forum/CarComplaints reports, and TSBs covering 2014-2016 especially). However, DAS was removed from the Q50 lineup for 2022+ model years, real DTCs are documented, and the severity rises to safety-critical given the recall and reports of steering lock-up/loss of assist.

title: VR30DDTT Turbo Heat Shield Rattle
issues: Cold-start rattle on VR30DDTT is far more commonly diagnosed as wastegate/turbo rattle (a known turbo-failure precursor), not loose heat shields - misattribution of root cause
Severity 'low' is miscalibrated if the true cause is wastegate rattle, which leads to limp mode and turbo replacement
Repair cost $50-$300 is wildly low if the actual issue is wastegate rattle requiring turbo replacement (typically $3,000-$6,000+ out of warranty)
Year range only applies to VR30DDTT-equipped trims (3.0t / Red Sport, 2016+); base Q50 2.0t and 3.7L trims do not have VR30DDTT
2026 model year is speculative/forward-looking
evidence: Multiple Q50 owner forum threads describe a cold-start rattle on VR30DDTT engines, but the overwhelming consensus (Infiniti Q50 Forum, Q60 Forum, Nissan Z Club) attributes it to electronic wastegate rattle inside the turbocharger assembly - which is non-serviceable and requires full turbo replacement - not loose exhaust/turbo heat shields. While loose heat shields do occur on Q50s generally, conflating the well-documented VR30DDTT wastegate rattle with a minor heat shield issue significantly understates severity and repair cost.

title: VR30DDTT Turbo Coolant Line Leak
issues: Specific failure mode (plastic quick-connect fittings on turbo coolant supply lines cracking from heat) is not documented for VR30DDTT - this failure pattern is associated with other engines like Ford 6.7 Powerstroke, Ford EcoBoost, and Alfa Romeo Giulia, not the Infiniti VR30DDTT

Actual documented VR30DDTT coolant issues are: porous engine blocks, water pump seal leaks (Infiniti TSB exists), multi-way control valve leaks, and internal turbo seal failures causing coolant to be consumed through the turbos
Year range incorrect: Infiniti Q60 production ended after 2022 model year; 2023-2026 Q60s do not exist

Repair cost range of $200-$800 is dramatically low for the actual documented VR30 coolant issues - turbo replacement, engine replacement, or multi-way control valve repairs typically run $1,500 to $30,000
Description appears to conflate generic 'turbo coolant line leak' failure modes from other vehicles with the VR30DDTT, which has different (and more serious) documented coolant failure patterns
evidence: Forum searches across Infiniti Q50/Q60 communities and an Infiniti TSB show the VR30DDTT's well-known coolant problems involve porous blocks, water pump seal leaks, multi-way control valve leaks, and internal turbo seal failures - not plastic quick-connect fittings on turbo coolant supply lines cracking. The described failure mode matches issues found on Ford EcoBoost/Powerstroke and Alfa Romeo Giulia engines instead.

title: Rear Air Suspension Compressor Failure
issues: The 2014-2019 Infiniti Q70 sedan was not offered from the factory with rear air suspension; it uses conventional coil-spring suspension with optional sport-tuned suspension or Dynamic Digital Suspension (DDS), none of which use air springs or a compressor
Rear air suspension compressor failure is a well-documented issue on Nissan Armada / Infiniti QX56 / QX80 SUVs, not on the Q70 sedan — the issue appears to have been confused between platforms
No NHTSA complaints, TSBs, or owner-forum threads describe OEM rear air suspension compressor failures on the Q70
DTC field is blank, but the related QX/Armada issue is associated with C1803 (exhaust solenoid) — irrelevant here since the Q70 has no such system
Repair cost range is plausible for the QX/Armada compressor (~$600-$1000 typical) but does not apply to a Q70
Severity/mileage claims cannot be validated because the underlying premise (Q70 having factory air suspension) is incorrect
evidence: Searches of Infiniti press materials, Edmunds, KBB, and owner forums confirm the Q70 sedan (2014-2019) was sold with conventional suspension and optional sport-tuned or DDS setups — not factory air suspension. Documented rear air suspension compressor failures (with C1803 codes) exist on the Nissan Armada / Infiniti QX56 / QX80 SUVs, suggesting the AI conflated platforms; aftermarket air suspension kits exist for the Q70 but are not an OEM 'known issue.'

title: Rear Hatch Strut Weakness and Power Liftgate Support Failure in Cold Weather
issues: 2014-2018 QX50 (first-gen, based on EX platform) did NOT have a power liftgate — power liftgate was only introduced on the 2019+ second-gen QX50, so the 'power-assisted liftgate' description does not apply to this year range
Issue description conflates two different generations; manual gas-strut weakness is real for 2014-2018, but power liftgate failures belong to 2019+
Severity 'low' is reasonable for manual strut weakness but understates 2019+ power liftgate spindle replacement cost (~$2,500+ at dealer)
Repair cost range $80-$450 fits manual struts (~$163-$174 per RepairPal) but is far too low if power liftgate spindles are included
evidence: Forum evidence confirms manual rear hatch gas struts weaken with age and groan in cold weather across Nissan/Infiniti vehicles, with RepairPal listing QX50 liftgate strut replacement at $163-$174. However, QX50 owners explicitly state the 2008-2017 (and carryover 2018) QX50 never had a power liftgate — that feature debuted on the 2019 redesign, making the 'power liftgate support failure' claim inapplicable to the 2014-2018 year range specified.

title: AC Compressor Premature Failure
issues: No documented widespread/premature AC compressor failure pattern specific to 2014-2020 QX60 — no recalls or TSBs found
Description frames normal wear-and-tear as a known systemic defect, which is misleading
Specific mileage range (60,000-80,000) and failure modes (clutch bearing + shaft seal leak) appear unsupported by sources; failures are described as generic wear
Year range 2014-2020 implies systemic issue across generation but no evidence supports this scope
Repair cost range $800-$1800 is plausible but the underlying premise of 'premature' failure is unsupported
evidence: Go-Parts (early 2026) explicitly states there are no specific recalls or widespread TSBs from Nissan/Infiniti for premature A/C compressor failure on the QX60/Pathfinder 3.5L V6, and failures are attributed to normal wear and tear. RepairPal and forum sources discuss AC compressor failure as a generic possible cause of AC problems across all QX60 model years (2014-2025), not as a known defect specific to 2014-2020.

title: Fuel Smell or Fuel Leak from Loose/Improperly Sealed Fuel Pump or Tank Components
issues: No NHTSA recall or manufacturer TSB found for a fuel pump or fuel tank sealing/leak issue on 2022-2023 Infiniti QX60
DTCs P0455/P0456 are EVAP system leak codes (gas cap/EVAP), not fuel pump sealing codes - mismatch with described 'fuel pump-related sealing' issue
Known 2022-2023 QX60 fuel pump complaints in owner forums describe pump failure/engine shutdown (no recall issued), not fuel odor/leakage
Description claims inclusion in a recall, but no such recall exists in NHTSA database for this issue
Repair cost range is speculative since the underlying issue/recall does not appear to exist (recall repairs would be $0 to owner)
evidence: Searches of NHTSA, cars.com, KBB, Infiniti USA recall pages, and QX60 owner forums show no fuel pump sealing or fuel leak/odor recall for 2022-2023 QX60. Documented recalls for these model years cover ABS, AFS headlights, second-row seats, driver seat rails, airbag inflators, and an A/C condenser pipe emission campaign - none involve fuel pump sealing or fuel tank leaks. Forum discussions reference fuel pump failures causing stalling, but Infiniti has not issued a recall for that either.

title: Transmission Judder at Low Speed
issues: Repair cost range ($150-$500) is dramatically understated; actual repairs range from ~$1,200 for valve body/torque converter to $4,500-$7,500+ for full CVT replacement
Severity likely undercalibrated - class action lawsuits and NHTSA complaints cite safety hazards (sudden power loss, risk of being rear-ended), suggesting high rather than medium
Speed range description slightly inaccurate - judder typically manifests at 15-40 mph under light throttle/uphill, not primarily parking lot maneuvers
DTC field lists 'none' but P17F1 and other CVT codes can appear in progressed cases (though early-stage judder often is codeless)
evidence: Multiple sources (CarComplaints, NHTSA complaints, Infiniti forums, class action lawsuits) confirm widespread CVT judder/shudder in 2013-2020 QX60 (Jatco CVT8). Infiniti issued TSBs (ITB13-037, ITB15-012) and a Stringer v. NNA settlement covered 2015-2018 models; typical repair costs run $1,200-$7,500, far exceeding the listed $150-$500.

title: VK56VD Timing Chain Stretch
issues: Year range is incorrect: the timing chain issue primarily affects 2011-2013 model years; Nissan updated the components when the vehicle was renamed QX80 in 2014, so 2014-2017 QX80s are largely unaffected
Vehicle naming inaccuracy: 2011-2013 model years were branded QX56, not QX80; QX80 branding began in 2014

Root cause mischaracterized: the issue stems from a design defect (weak chain/guide components related to the high-pressure fuel pump addition) addressed by a Nissan recall (Infiniti ID P6305), not primarily from neglected oil changes
Description omits the official Nissan/Infiniti voluntary recall issued May 2016 for affected vehicles
evidence: Multiple sources (Cars.com, Infiniti forums, Engine Patrol, Club Armada) confirm the VK56VD timing chain stretch issue is real but is specifically tied to 2011-2013 QX56/M56/Q70 models and was subject to an official Infiniti recall (P6305) in May 2016; Nissan updated the timing chain components when the vehicle was rebranded as QX80 in 2014, so the 2014-2017 QX80 model years listed are largely unaffected. DTC codes P0300 and P0011 are consistent with owner-reported symptoms, and repair costs of $2,000-$5,000 align with reported quotes (~$6,000 reported in one case, with labor alone running $1,200-$2,000+).

title: Air Suspension Compressor Failure
issues: DTC codes appear incorrect - documented codes for this issue are C2302 (levelling plausibility) and C2303 (reservoir plausibility), not C1A20/C1A13
Compressor manufacturer is Dunlop (OEM) on X350/X358; Hitachi association with XJ is not well documented in sources
Severity 'high' may be miscalibrated - multiple sources indicate the car remains drivable with the fault and it's primarily a comfort/cost issue rather than safety-critical

Year range 2004-2019 is broadly correct but conflates two different platforms (X350/X358 dry single-piston compressor 2004-2009 vs X351 2011-2019 with different compressor design where failures are less common)
evidence: The air suspension compressor failure is extremely well documented as the most common air suspension issue on the X350/X358 XJ, caused by a worn Teflon/phenolic piston ring leading to overwork and burnout, often exacerbated by leaking air springs. However, the trouble codes cited (C1A20, C1A13) do not match the documented codes (C2302, C2303), and forum/specialist sources indicate compressor failure is much rarer on the X351 (2011+) generation.

title: Timing Chain Tensioner Failure on AJ-V8
issues: Year range is wrong: timing chain tensioner failure is a well-known issue on the X308 XJ8 (1998-2000, some through mid-2001) with the early AJ26/AJ27 plastic tensioners, NOT the 2004-2015 XJ generations
The X350 (2004-2009) received the redesigned AJ28 4.2L engine with metal tensioners and Morse chains specifically to address this problem
The X351 (2010-2015) uses the 5.0L AJ133 V8 (or supercharged/diesel variants) which is a different engine family entirely and does not share this defect
DTC codes P0016/P0017 (cam/crank correlation) may set with severe chain stretch but are not the characteristic codes documented for this specific failure mode

Repair cost range ($4000-$9000) is high; documented owner reports for tensioner/chain work on affected cars cite roughly $1,500-$3,000, with full engine replacement after catastrophic failure being the high end
Severity 'high' is defensible due to catastrophic engine destruction risk, but it does not apply to the listed vehicle years
evidence: Multiple Jaguar owner forums, JCNA, and RepairPal document the plastic secondary timing chain tensioner failure as an AJ-V8 issue confined to 1997-2000/2001 XK8 and XJ8 (X308) models; Jaguar redesigned the timing system with metal tensioners for the AJ28 4.2L used in the X350 (2004+), and the X351 (2010+) uses entirely different engines. The described defect does not apply to the 2004-2015 XJ range stated in the entry.

title: Ingenium Engine Water Pump Failure
issues: DTC P26B7 is incorrect - it refers to 'Coolant Bypass Valve C Control Circuit/Open' (a solenoid circuit code, primarily a Ford code), not a water pump bearing/impeller mechanical failure which typically has no specific DTC and presents as low coolant warnings

Engine attribution is wrong - the well-documented F-PACE water pump failure issue is on the 3.0L supercharged V6 (AJ-V6, shared with F-Type/Land Rover), which is NOT an Ingenium engine; the Ingenium 2.0L's primary documented issue is timing chain wear, not water pump failure
Trim list (25t, 30t, R-Sport, S) covers 2.0L Ingenium variants but omits the 35t/S 3.0L V6 which is the trim actually affected by this issue
Repair cost range ($800-$1800) is low for dealer pricing on the 3.0L V6 where supercharger removal is often needed (forum reports of $3,600); range is reasonable for independent shops only
evidence: Forum reports (F-Pace Forum, Jaguar Forums) and UK specialist shops (K Motors, RCV) confirm water pump failures are common on the 3.0L supercharged V6 F-PACE, often involving the plastic crossover/Y-pipe and bearing corrosion, but this engine is the AJ-V6 not Ingenium. P26B7 is documented by KBB and Ford TSBs as a coolant bypass solenoid circuit fault, unrelated to mechanical water pump failure.

title: Ingenium Water Pump Premature Failure
issues: Water pump premature failure is documented primarily on Jaguar supercharged 3.0L V6 and 5.0L V8 engines, not specifically the 2.0L Ingenium as described
The 2.0L Ingenium's well-documented cooling issues are plastic coolant hoses/pipes, thermostat housing leaks, and piston cooling jet solenoid failures - not water pump bearing/impeller failure
DTC P26B7 could not be verified as a documented code for this specific failure on the XE Ingenium; common Ingenium DTCs are P0011, P000A, P0087, P228C
Description of 'bearing wear and impeller separation' as failure mode is not corroborated in sources for the 2.0L Ingenium
Severity 'high' is debatable - water pump failure is serious if ignored but typically gives warning (coolant warning, weep hole leak) before catastrophic overheating
evidence: Search results show the 2.0L Ingenium in the XE has well-documented timing chain, turbo, plastic coolant hose, and piston cooling solenoid issues, but water pump premature failure is specifically cited as a problem on supercharged 3.0 V6 and 5.0 V8 Jaguar engines (e.g., F-Pace 35t, XFR). Forum mentions of XE water pump issues often turn out to be plastic coolant pipes or thermostat housings rather than the pump itself.

title: Automatic Transmission Valve Body Wear
issues: Transmission identification is incorrect: 2000-2008 S-TYPE primarily used the Ford 5R55N (V6 and V8), not the ZF 5HP - the ZF 5HP24 was fitted to XJ8/XK8, not S-TYPE. Later S-TYPE (2003+) used ZF 6HP26 on some models
JF506E reference is likely wrong - S-TYPE V6 used the Ford 5R55N, not the Mazda/Ford JF506E (which was used in Jaguar X-TYPE)
DTC codes are generic; more commonly documented codes for this specific failure are P0745 (pressure control solenoid), P0734, P0735 (gear ratio specific)
Severity 'medium' is reasonable but repair cost range ($800-$2500) is narrow - DIY valve body spring repair can be under $50, while full transmission replacement runs $2500-$4000+
evidence: Jaguar TSB S307-19 confirms 2000-02 S-TYPE valve body/solenoid failures causing erratic/harsh shifts, and multiple forums document widespread 5R55N valve body wear (notably broken 4-3 prestroke valve springs) on S-TYPE. However, the ZF 5HP transmissions cited in the entry were used in the XJ8/XK8, not the S-TYPE, which used the Ford 5R55N across V6 and V8 trims for most of the model run.

title: Upper Touchscreen Delamination and Bubbling
issues: No evidence of touchscreen glass delamination/bubbling reported for Jaguar I-PACE in NHTSA, JLR TSBs, or owner forums
I-PACE infotainment complaints are overwhelmingly software-related (blank/black screens, reboots fixed by IMC/telematics updates), not physical glass delamination
Delamination/bubbling is a well-known issue on Stellantis Uconnect screens (Jeep/Dodge/Chrysler) and older Jaguar XF/XK units — appears to have been mistakenly attributed to the I-PACE
Repair cost field is blank; a real screen replacement would typically run $1,500–$2,000+
Severity 'low' would be questionable if real, since spreading delamination eventually impairs touch input and backup-camera visibility (typically medium)
evidence: Searches of I-PACE owner forums (i-paceforum.com, ipaceforums.co.uk), CarComplaints/JaguarForums TSB listings, and NHTSA-related sources show I-PACE touchscreen problems are software-driven blank/reboot issues resolved via IMC/telematics updates — no reports of glass-layer delamination or bubbling. Delamination/bubbling complaints in the search results pertain to Stellantis Uconnect units and a 2009–2011 Jaguar XF windshield TSB (JTB00193), not the I-PACE infotainment.

title: Electronic Throttle Body Failure on V6 Models
issues: S-Type V6 does NOT use GDI (gasoline direct injection); it uses sequential fuel injection (SFI) - the GDI claim is fabricated
Root cause is more commonly water ingress into the TPS connector and motor/sensor failure, not carbon buildup
Engine is the Jaguar AJ-V6 (AJ30) with Jaguar-designed heads, not simply the 'Ford-derived Duratec' - it's a derivative but distinct
Repair cost range ($150-$600) is significantly low; forum/dealer reports show $1,400-$2,000+ for throttle body replacement
Jaguar-specific DTCs commonly reported are P1229, P1121, P1580, P1584; P2135/P2101 are generic and less commonly cited for this specific failure
Year range slightly off - S-Type production ended 2007/2008, V6 introduced for 2000 MY; '2000-2008' is approximately correct but final year is debatable
Severity arguably should be 'high' since sudden limp mode at highway speeds (documented at 90 mph) is a safety concern
evidence: Multiple Jaguar owner forums extensively document throttle body / 'Failsafe Engine Mode' failures on S-Type V6 models, typically attributed to water intrusion into the TPS connector rather than carbon buildup, with dealer repair costs commonly reported in the $1,400-$2,000 range. The engine is the Jaguar AJ-V6 (AJ30), based on the Ford Duratec architecture but with Jaguar-specific SFI fuel injection - it does not have GDI as claimed.

title: Coolant Crossover Pipe Leak on Supercharged V6
issues: Repair cost range ($600-$1400) is significantly understated; real-world costs typically run $2,000-$3,900 because supercharger removal is required

Failure mechanism described inaccurately: primary failure mode is cracking/splitting of brittle plastic pipes (Y-pipe, upper/lower coolant outlet pipes), not O-ring seal degradation at the supercharger connection

Vehicle scope error: F-PACE SVR uses the 5.0L supercharged V8 (AJ133), not the 3.0L supercharged V6 — though the V8 has analogous plastic coolant pipe failures, so SVR inclusion is defensible but the engine reference is wrong
Severity arguably understated: owners report catastrophic failures with no warning leading to overheating; could be argued medium-to-high rather than medium
Description says leak is 'difficult to detect visually' which is partially accurate (leaks into engine valley under supercharger), but this should be noted as a key diagnostic detail
evidence: Multiple Jaguar F-PACE owner forums (fpaceforum.com, jaguarforums.com) and independent repair sources extensively document plastic coolant crossover/Y-pipe failures on 2017+ supercharged 3.0L V6 F-PACEs, with Jaguar having redesigned the parts and aluminum aftermarket replacements available. Reported repair costs consistently fall in the $2,000-$3,900 range due to required supercharger removal, well above the stated $600-$1400.

title: Rear Differential Mount Bushing Premature Wear
issues: Misdescribes the actual issue: documented F-PACE problem is cracked differential housing/mounting brackets and internal differential (pinion gear) failure, not rubber bushing wear
Repair cost severely underestimated: real-world quotes are $3,000-$4,800 for differential replacement, not $300-$900
Severity likely miscategorized as 'low' - owners report complete differential failure requiring full replacement, which is a medium/high cost issue
Symptom description is partially inaccurate: owners report whining/drumming/grinding noises and detected cracks, not just clunking on accel/decel transitions
TSBs exist for related issues (rear differential pinion gear manufactured out of spec, pinion seal leaks, rear creak noise) but none specifically for 'mount bushing wear'
evidence: Forum owners and TSBs confirm F-PACE (especially 2017) has documented rear differential problems, but the actual issue is cracked cast-aluminum differential housing/brackets and pinion gear failure requiring full diff replacement at $3K-$4.8K, not simple bushing wear at $300-$900. Jaguar TSBs reference rear differential pinion gear manufacturing defects and pinion seal leaks, not mount bushing wear specifically.

title: Turbo Coolant Hose Failure on Ingenium Engine
issues: Turbo coolant feed/return hose failure as described is documented on the 3.0L I6 Ingenium engine, not the 2.0L Ingenium
The well-documented 2.0L Ingenium coolant issue is the thermostat housing leaking onto the piston cooling oil jet solenoid, not turbo hoses
Real 2.0L Ingenium turbo failures are caused by oil starvation/contamination, not coolant hose cracking
Description appears to conflate the 3.0L turbo coolant hose issue with the 2.0L engine
Repair cost range ($300-$800) may be low; documented Jaguar coolant hose repairs frequently run $1,500-$2,500 when supercharger/access work is involved (though that's V6, not 2.0L)
Year range 2016-2023 is plausible for the 2.0L Ingenium in XF (X260), but issue itself is misattributed
evidence: Documented sources (K Motors, Apex Engines, Green's Garage) identify the 2.0L Ingenium's main coolant-related fault as thermostat housing leakage onto the piston cooling solenoid, and plastic coolant pipes cracking generally - not specifically turbocharger coolant feed/return hoses. The turbo coolant hose failure pattern described matches the 3.0L I6 Ingenium engine, not the 2.0L four-cylinder.

title: Nikasil Cylinder Bore Wear on Early AJ-V8
issues: Year range is entirely wrong: Nikasil bores were only used 1996-August 2000; Jaguar switched to steel liners on 18/08/2000, well before any 2007-2011 X150 XK existed
The 4.2L AJ-V8 (introduced for 2003 MY) never used Nikasil coatings - it always had steel liners
2007-2011 XK (X150 generation) is entirely unaffected by this issue - applies to the prior X100 XK8/XKR generation only
DTC codes P0300/P0301/P0302 are generic misfire codes and not specifically associated/documented with Nikasil bore wear diagnosis (which is identified by blow-by testing, not OBD codes)
Repair cost range may be low; Nikasil-damaged blocks cannot be rebored and typically require full engine replacement
Severity rating arguably overstated - causes drivability issues/engine failure but not a sudden safety-critical failure
evidence: Multiple authoritative sources (Jaguar forums, Jag-lovers, Underhood Service, Motorious) confirm Nikasil cylinder coatings were used only on AJ-V8 engines built before 18 August 2000, after which Jaguar switched to steel liners. The issue affected 1996-1999/2000 XK8/XKR (X100) and contemporary XJ/S-Type, not the 2007-2011 XK (X150) which uses the later 4.2L AJ-V8 with steel liners exclusively.

title: Turbo Coolant Hose Failure on Ingenium Engine
issues: The specific failure mode described (turbo coolant hoses splitting near turbo housing) is not a documented common issue for the E-PACE; documented E-PACE coolant leaks center on thermostat housing, coolant separator, water pump, and plastic coolant pipes/crossover Y-pipe

The 'turbo coolant hose' failure pattern is more strongly associated with the 3.0L I6 Ingenium (used in other JLR vehicles) and the 3.0L supercharged V6 in F-PACE/F-Type, not the 2.0L Ingenium in the E-PACE

Repair cost range of $250-$700 appears low; owner-reported E-PACE coolant hose repairs run ~£500/$600+ at minimum, and related JLR coolant hose jobs often exceed $2,000 due to intake/supercharger removal labor
No JLR TSB specifically identifies 'turbo coolant hose' failure on E-PACE as described
evidence: Forum reports (epaceforum.com, jaguarforum.com) and shop guides (K Motors) document E-PACE coolant leaks primarily from the coolant separator, thermostat housing, water pump, and plastic coolant pipes — not turbo coolant hoses specifically. The turbo coolant hose failure pattern matches the 3.0L I6 Ingenium and 3.0L supercharged V6 (F-PACE/F-Type) per Green's Garage and JLR TSB JTB00566, not the 2.0L Ingenium in the E-PACE.

title: Exhaust Manifold Crack on Supercharged V6
issues: No documented pattern of cast-iron exhaust manifold cracking on the F-TYPE 3.0L supercharged V6 in TSBs, NHTSA complaints, or major owner-forum/specialist common-fault lists
Known F-TYPE V6 common issues are timing chain tensioner/guide failure, water pump failure, and active exhaust valve failure — not manifold cracking
Manifold-cracking issues in Jaguar lore are associated with older diesel models (X351 3.0D, S-Type 2.7D), not the AJ126 supercharged petrol V6
Cost range lower bound ($500) is optimistic; RepairPal estimates F-Type exhaust manifold replacement at roughly $1,719-$1,960
Description conflates generic 'ticking + exhaust smell' symptoms with a specific failure mode not substantiated for this engine
evidence: Specialist common-fault write-ups for the F-TYPE (e.g., K Motors) and engine-issue summaries for the 3.0 V6 supercharged do not list exhaust manifold cracking; recurring issues cited are timing chain jumping, water pump failure, and active exhaust valve seizure. Cracked exhaust manifolds in Jaguar forums are discussed in the context of older diesel engines, not the F-TYPE's AJ126 supercharged V6.

title: High-Voltage Contactor Failure Warning
issues: DTC P0AA6 is incorrect for the described issue - P0AA6 is an HV Battery Voltage System Isolation Fault, not a contactor failure code
Correct DTCs for contactor failures would be P0AA0 (positive contactor), P0ADD (negative contactor), P0AE1 (precharge contactor), or P3051 (contactor C)
Description conflates two distinct issues: isolation faults (P0AA6, most commonly reported on I-PACE) vs. actual contactor failures
Repair cost range ($1000-$3500) appears low - real-world cases show £1,500+ parts with 12+ hours labor, dealer diagnostics alone £1,770, and full repairs reaching £7,000-£13,000
Cause described (degradation from cycling/arcing) does not match the typical P0AA6 root causes documented (corrosion in HV connections, base plate, BECM/BEM issues, cell isolation breakdown)
evidence: Jaguar's own SSM74274 TSB lists P0AA6 as 'Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage System Isolation Fault' - separate from contactor codes P0AA0, P0ADD, P0AE1, P3051. Forum reports across 2019-2022 I-PACE models confirm P0AA6 is common but relates to HV isolation/leak current between 12V and 400V systems, often caused by base plate, BECM, harness, or cell issues - with repairs frequently exceeding the stated cost range.

title: OEM Tire Tread Separation and Blowout Risk
issues: Continental tire tread separation complaints in NHTSA are for the Jaguar X-Type (sedan/Sportwagon), not the XK grand tourer
No NHTSA complaints, TSBs, or recalls found for tire tread separation specifically on the 2006 Jaguar XK
The only tire-related recall affecting XK is for 2007-2009 model years (TPMS non-compliance), not 2006 and not tread separation
Severity rating may be justified IF the issue existed, but the issue itself is misattributed to the wrong vehicle model
Repair cost range is plausible for tire replacement but irrelevant since the issue is misattributed
Source claim 'nhtsa-verified' is misleading — NHTSA data supports X-Type complaints, not XK
evidence: NHTSA complaints describing OEM Continental ContiProContact/ContiTouring tread separation and blowouts on Jaguars specifically reference the 2006 Jaguar X-Type sedan and Sportwagon (225/45R17 tires), not the XK coupe/convertible. The 2006 Jaguar XK has only one NHTSA recall on record (an unrelated accelerator pedal issue), with no documented pattern of OEM tire tread separation complaints for that model.

title: Automatic Transmission or Transfer Case Failure
issues: Vehicle misidentified: 2006 Jaguar XK is RWD coupe/convertible and has no transfer case — transfer case failures apply to the AWD Jaguar X-Type, a different model
Cited complaints (catastrophic transmission + transfer case failure, gears fragmented) are from 2006 X-Type owners, not XK owners
NHTSA shows only 1 recall for 2006 XK and it relates to the accelerator pedal, not transmission/gearbox
No documented Jaguar recall on 2006 XK for 'reverse selected while forward chosen' gearbox condition
DTC field is empty for an issue that, if real, would typically log transmission/gearbox fault codes (e.g., gearbox fault lamp / P-codes)
Repair cost range is plausible for X-Type ($4,000–$6,500 reported) but not validated for the XK platform
evidence: NHTSA complaints and forum threads about catastrophic automatic transmission and transfer case failures (gears fragmented, no movement) are documented for the AWD Jaguar X-Type, not the 2006 XK, which is RWD and has no transfer case. The only NHTSA recall for the 2006 XK concerns the accelerator pedal assembly, and the second-generation XK launched in 2006 for MY2007 — the issue appears to conflate two different Jaguar models.

title: Coolant Crossover Pipe Leak Under Intake Manifold
issues: Wrong engines specified: the infamous coolant crossover pipe failure is on the 5.0L V8 (supercharged and NA, 2010+), not the BMW 4.4L M62 (2003-2005) or Jaguar/Ford AJ-V8 4.4L (2006-2009)

Year range is significantly off: the documented widespread issue starts with 2010 model year 5.0L engines, not 2006-2009 4.4L vehicles; range should likely be 2010-2013 for L322 (and continues into L405)
Failure mechanism description is incorrect: pipes fail due to plastic cracking from heat cycling, not O-ring leaks or 'electrolysis corroding pipe from inside out' (pipes are plastic, not metal)
TDV8 4.4L diesel is mentioned but the prominent forum-documented failure is on gasoline 5.0L, not the TDV8 (TDV8 has different coolant pipe issues)
Repair cost range is on the low side: dealer quotes are commonly $2,000-$4,300; indie shops $1,500-$2,200 is more typical, so $800 floor is unrealistic
evidence: Forum sources (rangerovers.net, landroverworld.org) extensively document the coolant crossover pipe failure as a well-known issue on the 5.0L V8 (2010+) Range Rover/Sport/LR4, where plastic pipes under the supercharger/intake crack and cause sudden coolant loss and catastrophic engine overheating. The issue described (O-ring leaks on metal pipes due to electrolysis) does not match the documented plastic-pipe-cracking failure mode, and the specified BMW 4.4L V8 and 2006-2009 AJ-V8 4.4L engines are not the engines associated with this widespread failure.

title: Terrain Response System Faults and Mode Selection Failure
issues: DTC P1889 is associated with the Haldex Active On-Demand Coupling used on Freelander 2/Evoque/Discovery Sport, not the LR3/LR4 transfer case described in the issue
Description conflates two different drivetrain systems: LR3/LR4 has a true 2-speed transfer case (shift motor failure is real), while P1889 refers to a different platform's Haldex coupling oil pump
U0102 (Lost Communication with Transfer Case Control Module) and C1A00 are plausible but not specifically corroborated as the documented codes for this LR3/LR4 issue
Year range 2005-2016 spans both LR3 (2005-2009) and LR4 (2010-2016) which is acceptable, though the 'Discovery' nameplate was not used in the US during these years
Severity 'medium' is reasonable since vehicle remains drivable; cost range $300-$1800 is plausible (switch pack ~$1200 reported on forums)
evidence: Forums confirm Terrain Response faults, stuck modes, rotary switch pack failures, and transfer case actuator issues are well-documented on LR3/LR4. However, the Land Rover TSB LTB00795NAS1 and Haldex repair sources confirm DTC P1889-14 refers to the Active On-Demand Coupling oil pump brushes on Freelander 2/Evoque (Gen 4 Haldex, 2008-2015), a fundamentally different AWD system than the LR3/LR4 transfer case.

title: Transfer Case Actuator Motor and Chain Failure
issues: Transfer case manufacturer is incorrect: L320 uses Magna Steyr (DD295), not BorgWarner
DTC P1889 is not commonly associated with this issue on L320; typical codes are P0806, P0915, P186D, P181D
DTC U0102 (Lost Communication with TCCM) is a generic communication code, not specific to actuator/chain failure
Chain stretch failure mode is not a well-documented issue on the Magna Steyr DD295 unit; actuator/shift motor and clutch position sensor failures dominate forum reports
Severity 'high' may be overstated — typically results in loss of low-range/4WD function rather than safety-critical failure
evidence: Forum evidence (rangerovers.net, aulro.com) confirms transfer case shift motor/actuator failures on L320 are common, but the unit is Magna Steyr DD295 (not BorgWarner), and reported DTCs are P0806, P0915, P186D, P181D — not P1889/U0102. Repair costs (~$1000+ for actuator, multi-thousand for rebuild) are in the right range.

title: Exterior Door Handle Mechanism Failure
issues: First-generation Evoque (2012-2019) does NOT have pop-out/retractable door handles; those are on the Velar and second-gen Evoque (2020+)
Description of mechanism (pop-out, micro-switches, spring mechanism) is incorrect for this generation
Actual common issue on 2012-2019 Evoque is door lock/latch actuator failure with conventional handles, not handle mechanism failure
DTC codes listed as 'none' but real-world actuator failures often throw B1161/B1166/B1167 codes
Repair cost range $300-$800 is roughly plausible for actuator replacement at a shop but DIY parts are ~$30-50
evidence: Forum and repair sources confirm 2012-2019 Evoques have conventional (non-retractable) door handles, with the common failure being the internal door lock/latch actuator (around £300/$300+ at a garage, ~$30-50 DIY part). Pop-out/retractable handles only appear on the Velar (2018+) and second-generation Evoque (2020+), so the entry's described mechanism does not exist on the listed model years.

title: Haldex AWD Coupling Failure
issues: Haldex generation is wrong: Evoque uses Gen 4 Haldex, not Gen 5; the most-cited code in forums/repair sources is P1889, not the listed U0300/C1A54

Year range likely too broad: starting in 2014 the Evoque switched from Haldex to a GKN active/standard driveline, so 2014-2019 AWD models are not Haldex-equipped (issue mainly affects 2012-2013, possibly early 2014)

Described failure mode is partially inaccurate: forums attribute failures primarily to filter clogging and pump failure (no manufacturer-specified service interval), not 'overheating and electronic controller failure'
Repair cost range is plausible but on the low side for full coupling replacement (forum quotes ~£1,900/$2,400+ for new unit), while a fluid/filter service is ~$500-$780
evidence: Multiple owner forums and Land Rover specialists confirm Haldex coupling/pump failures are a well-known Evoque issue caused by neglected fluid/filter changes, with symptoms like 'Transmission Fault/Traction Reduced' and loss of rear drive. However, sources indicate the Evoque uses Gen 4 Haldex (not Gen 5), the common DTC is P1889, and from 2014 model year onward Land Rover replaced the Haldex with a GKN driveline, narrowing the affected range.

title: Electric Parking Brake Actuator Failure
issues: DTC codes are wrong: actual codes per TSB SSM74004 are C2005, C2006, C2007, C2008 (actuator stuck codes). C0044 is a brake pressure sensor code and C0055 relates to wheel speed/steering sensor — neither is the EPB actuator code

Root cause description is partially inaccurate: TSB SSM74004 identifies software corruption (release command interrupted by apply command) and mechanical gear failure as primary causes, not road salt/moisture corrosion
Repair cost upper bound is low: real-world owner reports commonly total $1300-$2500 (actuator ~$800-$1000 + ~6 hours labor); $1800 ceiling is borderline
Severity arguably understated: a stuck or non-holding parking brake on a 5,000+ lb SUV has safety implications, though 'medium' is defensible since the service brake still functions
evidence: Land Rover TSB SSM74004 (filed with NHTSA) confirms the EPB calibration/actuator stuck issue on L494 Range Rover Sport with specific DTCs C2005-71, C2006-71, C2007-72, and C2008-72 — not C0044/C0055. Multiple owner forums (LandRoverWorld, RangeRovers.net, AULRO) confirm widespread actuator failures with repair costs typically $1000-$2500 including parts (~$450-$1000) and ~6 hours labor.

title: 2.0L Ingenium Engine Excessive Vibration at Idle
issues: No documented widespread 'excessive vibration at idle' issue specific to Defender 2.0L Ingenium; owner reports generally describe the P300 as smooth and well-dampened
Factual error: Defender L663 (2020+) uses a monocoque/unibody D7x aluminum platform, NOT body-on-frame as claimed
The comparison premise (body-on-frame Defender vs monocoque Evoque/Discovery Sport) is invalid since all three are unibody
Documented Ingenium idle issues are tied to PCV valve/oil separator failures causing rough idle/misfire, not generalized engine-mount vibration
Early engine mount failures on Defender P300 are not a commonly reported pattern in forums or TSBs
Repair cost range is speculative with no documented basis for this specific 'issue'
evidence: Searches of owner forums (Land Rover Forums, VW Vortex, Defender2.net) and Ingenium engine problem databases show the P300 is widely described as smooth and refined; documented idle complaints trace to PCV/oil-separator failures or timing chain issues, not chassis-amplified 4-cylinder vibration. The entry also contains a fundamental factual error claiming the Defender is body-on-frame when it actually uses JLR's D7x monocoque aluminum architecture.

title: Terrain Response ECU Software Glitches
issues: DTC U0102 is 'Lost Communication with Drive Motor Control Module A' and is not the standard code associated with Terrain Response faults; typical codes are U0001, U0073, U0122, U0128, U0155, U0300
C1A00 appears in VDM (Vehicle Dynamics Module) contexts as a generic 'Control Module' code, not specifically a Terrain Response ECU corruption code

Root cause mischaracterized: documented Terrain Response faults are overwhelmingly caused by subsystem faults (Haldex, ABS, transfer case, parking brake, battery voltage, water ingress at TCCM, steering angle sensor) — not 'ECU software corruption' or 'calibration data loss'
Year range 2005-2020 conflates three distinct platforms (LR3 2005-2009, LR4 2010-2016, L462 2017+); behavior and fixes differ significantly between them
No repair cost provided; real-world fixes range from free (steering angle recalibration, battery replacement) to $1,500+ (Haldex, transfer case actuator)
No NHTSA TSB or recall specifically for 'Terrain Response ECU software corruption' was identified
evidence: Forum threads and the LR workshop manual confirm Terrain Response 'Special Programs Not Available' warnings are common across LR3/LR4/Discovery Sport, but they are subsystem-driven (battery, Haldex, TCCM water ingress, steering angle sensor, CAN bus loss) rather than ECU software corruption with the cited DTCs. The codes U0102 and C1A00 do not align with the standard set of communication/TR codes seen in real diagnostic reports (U0001, U0073, U0122, U0128, U0155, U0300).

title: Water Ingress into Tailgate and Rear Light Clusters
issues: Velar does not have a 'continuous LED tail light strip that spans the tailgate' - it has separate side tail light clusters plus a center lamp panel; the description conflates Velar with newer full-width light bar designs
Condensation in Land Rover tail lights is documented by JLR as normal/expected behavior due to Goretex breather membranes, not a defect
No evidence found of widespread Velar-specific water ingress causing LED failure, wiper motor damage, or liftgate actuator failure as a cascading issue
No TSBs or NHTSA complaints found specifically targeting Velar tailgate water ingress with the described symptoms
Repair cost range is speculative without a documented repair pattern; tail lamp assembly alone can exceed the upper bound
evidence: Forum discussions for the Velar treat tail light condensation as expected behavior per the owner's manual, not a defect. While water ingress around tailgate seals/rear lights is a known pattern on older Land Rovers (Evoque, L322), there is no strong documented evidence of a chronic Velar-specific issue matching the description's cascading damage to LEDs, wiper motors, and liftgate actuators.

title: L462 Discovery Air Suspension Height Sensor Failure
issues: DTC codes C1A20 and C1A23 do not match commonly documented Land Rover height sensor codes (typically C1A04/C1A05/C1A06 for front/rear height sensors, or C1A74 for sensor mechanism)
Height sensor failure is described as a less common failure mode on L462 compared to air spring leaks and compressor burnout, so framing it as 'particularly prone to failure' overstates frequency
Severity 'medium' is reasonable but could arguably be higher since a fault often locks the vehicle into 'Normal Height Only' mode affecting off-road capability
evidence: Forum posts and repair guides confirm height sensors on Land Rover Discovery/L462 can fail and cause uneven ride height, but documented DTCs for the four corner height sensors are C1A04-C1A06 and C1A74-range codes, not C1A20/C1A23. Sources also indicate height sensor failures are less common than air spring leaks or compressor failures on the L462.

title: Optional Air Suspension Faults After Off-Road Use
issues: DTC C1A20 is a generic Land Rover compressor fault code ('pressure increases too slow when filling reservoir') primarily documented on LR3/LR4/Disco 3-4/Range Rover L322/Sport platforms, not specifically tied to the L663 Defender or to the described mud/debris/puncture scenario
C1A20 relates to compressor/reservoir filling problems, not height sensor mud contamination or air spring puncture as described - DTCs do not match the failure mode

Claim that air suspension is 'standard on 110 V8 and X models' is too narrow; electronic air suspension is standard on additional L663 trims (e.g., First Edition, XS, and most six-cylinder configurations)
No repair cost provided; typical air suspension repairs range from ~$200 (sensor) to $2,000+ (full overhaul)
evidence: Owner forums and independent shops confirm L663 Defenders do experience air suspension issues including height sensor faults, compressor noise, and premature air strut wear, particularly with off-road use. However, DTC C1A20 is overwhelmingly documented on older Land Rover models (LR3/LR4, Disco 3/4, RR L322, RR Sport) as a compressor/reservoir pressure-rise fault, not as a mud/puncture-related code on the L663 Defender.

title: Rear Quarter Window Spontaneous Cracking
issues: The well-documented spontaneous cracking issue on the 2020+ Defender is the windshield, not the rear quarter window — no substantial evidence of rear quarter glass spontaneously cracking
Class action lawsuit (filed 2022, expanded 2024) specifically concerns windshields on 2020-2022 Defenders, not rear quarter glass

Rear quarter area issues that do exist are different problems: cosmetic rear quarter trim/panel popping off its clips, and the rear door fixed window assembly coming loose — neither involves spontaneous glass cracking
Repair cost of $500-$1500 is low for Defender glass work; windshield replacements are reported around $2,000-$2,471, though a smaller quarter glass might be cheaper if the issue were real
Year range 2020-2025 likely too broad — documented complaints/lawsuit primarily cover 2020-2022 model years
Severity 'low' may understate the issue if conflated with the windshield problem, which plaintiffs argue is a safety hazard
evidence: Extensive forum discussion, NHTSA complaints, and a US District Court class action lawsuit document spontaneous WINDSHIELD cracking on 2020-2022 Defenders attributed to thermal/design issues, with some owners replacing 3-5 windshields. No comparable body of evidence exists for rear quarter window glass spontaneously cracking — rear-area complaints involve trim panels detaching or fixed window assemblies loosening, not glass fracture.

title: Wade Sensing System False Alarms
issues: No documented evidence of wade sensing false alarms on Velar in NHTSA, TSBs, or owner forums
Wade sensing only activates during actual water wading, not from puddles or rain as described
Wade sensing is a rarely-optioned feature (not available in US for most years), making widespread issue claims implausible
Description conflates wade sensing with general moisture/puddle detection, which is not how the system works
evidence: Wade sensing is a real optional Velar feature using ultrasonic sensors in the door mirrors, but extensive searches of owner forums (velarforums.co.uk), NHTSA, and TSB databases found no documented pattern of false alarms from contaminated sensors. The described trigger mechanism (puddles/rain causing dashboard warnings) misrepresents how the system actually operates.

title: Front Door Check Strap Premature Wear
issues: No evidence of front door check strap premature wear on 2020-2024 L663 Defender; this is a known issue on classic/pre-2016 Defenders, not the new model
Documented door issues on the new Defender involve latch/actuator failures and seal suction, not check straps
Claim that 110 is worse 'due to larger doors' is incorrect - 90 and 110 share the same front door size/construction on L663
Repair cost range is speculative with no TSB or shop data to support it
Description appears to conflate well-known classic Defender check strap problems with the modern L663 platform
evidence: Forum searches on the L663 Defender (landroverforums.com, 2020-2024 model years) surface door problems related to electronic latches/actuators, child-lock glitches, and door-seal suction, but no reports of front door check strap wear. Check strap wear results all reference the pre-2016 classic Defender with two-piece doors, which is a structurally different vehicle.

title: Ingenium 2.0L High-Pressure Fuel Pump Cam Follower Wear
issues: Conflates two different engines: HPFP cam follower wear is a documented issue on the Ford-sourced 2.0L (pre-Ingenium) used in 2015-2017 Discovery Sport and 2012-2017 Evoque, NOT the JLR Ingenium 2.0L used in 2020-2025 Discovery Sport
The 2020-2025 Discovery Sport Ingenium engine's documented issues are timing chain stretch, oil dilution, turbo failures and DPF/VVT problems — not HPFP cam follower wear
No TSB, NHTSA complaint, or forum evidence found tying HPFP cam follower wear to the Ingenium engine specifically
Claim that JLR 'acknowledged with an updated part' for this specific issue on Ingenium engines is unsubstantiated
Year range (2020-2025) is wrong for the actual cam follower issue, which affected earlier Ford-engine model years
evidence: Search results confirm HPFP cam follower wear is a well-known issue on the Ford-derived 2.0L EcoBoost-based engine in 2015-2017 Discovery Sport and 2012-2017 Evoque, but the 2020-2025 Discovery Sport uses the JLR Ingenium 2.0L, whose documented problems are timing chain stretch, oil dilution, and turbo/VVT issues rather than HPFP cam follower wear. The entry appears to incorrectly transfer the older Ford engine's known issue to the newer Ingenium engine.

title: Wade Sensing System False Alerts and Calibration Issues
issues: Wade sensing does not auto-activate or alert during normal driving/rain/puddles - it must be manually selected from the 4x4 infotainment menu, so 'false alerts during rain' and 'distracting during normal driving' is technically inaccurate
System auto-disables above 6 mph and requires ~6 inches of water to register, contradicting the 'shallow puddle false alerts' claim
No NHTSA complaints, recalls, or TSBs found documenting this as a widespread issue
Only isolated forum reports of sensor misreads exist (often related to dirty sensors or folded mirrors per owner's manual), not a documented systemic defect
Description conflates a normal limitation/maintenance item (keep sensors clean) with a defect
Severity 'low' is reasonable IF the issue existed, but the issue as described doesn't match real-world behavior
evidence: Forum threads on landroverforums.com show isolated owner reports of wade sensors occasionally misreading, with causes traced to dirty sensors, folded mirrors, or insufficient water depth - all documented as normal limitations in the owner's manual. The system must be manually activated and disables above 6 mph, so the described 'false alerts in rain/puddles during normal driving' scenario is not how the system operates.

title: 48V Mild-Hybrid Battery / DC-DC Converter Fault Causing No-Start, Warning Messages, and Limp Mode
issues: DTC codes appear incorrect/fabricated - actual documented JLR DTC for this issue is P0A78-49 stored in the EPIC module per SSM76229/SSM76347, not P0A94/P1AEE/B11DB
U3000 is a generic communication code referenced in a different L461 TSB (air suspension/EESM), not specifically this 48V/DC-DC fault

TSBs (SSM76229, SSM76347) explicitly cite L460 Range Rover and L663 Defender; L461 Range Rover Sport inclusion is plausible due to shared MLA-Flex architecture but not directly confirmed in TSB text found
Description references 'battery energy control module (BECM)' which is more commonly associated with older L494 MHEV platform; new L461 uses EPIC module terminology
evidence: Multiple JLR TSBs filed with NHTSA in 2025 (SSM76173, SSM76229, SSM76347) confirm a real 'Stop Safely Electrical Fault Detected' issue tied to 48V DC-DC converter / EPIC module failures on L460/L663 MHEV vehicles, with documented DTC P0A78-49; owner forums and carproblemzoo report identical symptoms (sudden shutdown, electrical fault warnings, no-start) on Range Rover Sport MHEVs. However, the specific DTC codes listed in the entry do not match the actual JLR-documented code.

title: Front Brake Squeal, Judder, and Premature Rotor/Pads Replacement on Heavy New-Generation Models
issues: Issue is predominantly REAR brakes, not front as described - this is a significant misattribution
Root cause is torque vectoring by braking and rear brake bias (rear caliper doubles as e-brake), not front pad compound or wheel/tire weight
Repair costs understated - documented owner bills are $2,000-$2,500+, exceeding the $600-$1,800 range
Year range is reasonable but issue is most documented on 2023-2024 MY; some sources extend to 2022-2025
Severity arguably should be higher given active class action lawsuit alleging safety risk and potential brake system failure
evidence: An April 2026 class action lawsuit (Zats v. JLR NA) and extensive owner forum reports confirm premature brake wear on 2023+ Range Rover/Range Rover Sport, but the documented problem is rear pads/rotors wearing at 8,000-17,000 miles due to rear brake bias and torque vectoring by braking - not front brakes as described. Repair costs in the lawsuit run $2,000-$2,500+ per incident, above the stated range.

title: Water Intrusion from Tailgate / Rear Body Seals Causing Damp Cargo Area and Electrical Faults
issues: No documented TSBs, recalls, or widespread owner reports specifically about tailgate/rear body seal water intrusion on the 2023-2025 L461 Range Rover Sport
Forum reports of rear cargo water leaks are from older Range Rover Sport generations (L320/L494), not the redesigned L461
DTC 'B1DXX' is not a valid code - it is a wildcard placeholder, suggesting AI fabrication
U0140 (Lost Communication with BCM) is a generic communication code not specifically tied to water intrusion in the rear of this vehicle
Documented electrical faults on 2023+ Sport relate to DCDC converter/EPIC module (P0A78-49), not rear water ingress
Repair cost range is plausible in general but not anchored to any documented repair for this specific issue
evidence: NHTSA TSBs for the 2023+ L461 Range Rover Sport address MHEV DCDC converter failures and EPIC module faults rather than tailgate water intrusion, and forum reports of rear cargo water leaks reference older L320/L494 generations. The cited DTC 'B1DXX' is a placeholder rather than a real code, indicating the entry was likely AI-generated without source verification.

title: Excessive Oil Consumption 2GR Engine
issues: Conflates the well-documented 2AZ-FE (4-cyl) piston ring oil consumption issue with the 2GR-FE V6 — the 2GR-FE is not widely known for piston-ring oil consumption
No known Toyota TSB exists for 2GR-FE piston ring replacement to address oil consumption (the TSB applies to the 2AZ-FE)
The actual documented 2GR-FE issues in this RX350 range are timing cover oil leaks (2007-2009 mainly) and the rubber VVT-i oil supply hose rupture — both are leaks, not consumption
Consumption rate of 'quart every 1,500-3,000 miles' is the figure cited for 2AZ-FE litigation, not 2GR-FE
Repair cost range $200-$4000 is overly broad and not well calibrated; a piston ring/short block job on a 2GR-FE typically runs much higher
Severity 'medium' is reasonable if the issue existed, but the described issue itself is largely misattributed
evidence: Multiple specialist sources (CARspec, BobIsTheOilGuy, ToyotaNation, ClubLexus) document that the 2GR-FE V6 in 2007-2017 RX350s is primarily affected by timing cover oil leaks and rubber VVT-i oil line failures, not by piston-ring-driven oil consumption. The piston ring/TSB oil consumption issue with the 'quart per 1,200 miles' figure is documented for the 2AZ-FE four-cylinder engine (Camry, RAV4, Scion tC, etc.), not the 2GR-FE V6.

title: Dashboard Melting and Sticky Surface
issues: Wrong customer support program code: actual program is ZLD, not ZE7 (ZE7 is the Toyota 2AZ oil consumption program)
Year range too broad: official ZLD coverage is only 2006-2008 IS 250/350, not 2006-2013
IS F inclusion not supported by the warranty enhancement program documentation
Severity arguably understated: NHTSA/news reports describe windshield glare as a safety concern, not just cosmetic
evidence: The melting/sticky dashboard issue is well-documented via Lexus Warranty Enhancement Program ZLD, covering 2006-2008 IS 250/350 (plus other Lexus models like ES 350, GX 470, RX 330/350/400h, LS 460). The program code cited in the entry (ZE7) actually refers to a separate Toyota 4-cylinder oil consumption program, and the 2006-2013 year range and IS F inclusion exceed the documented coverage.

title: Excessive Oil Consumption 2GR-FE Engine
issues: The 2GR-FE V6 is not widely documented as having a piston-ring oil consumption defect; the well-known Toyota piston-ring oil consumption TSB applies to the 2AZ-FE 4-cylinder (Camry/RAV4/Scion), not the 2GR-FE V6

No Toyota/Lexus TSB acknowledging revised piston rings for the 2GR-FE could be verified; the actual 2GR-FE known issues are timing cover oil LEAKS (2007-2009) and VVT-i oil line rupture (LSC campaign on 2007-2008 ES350)

The piston-ring oil-burning issue commonly attributed to Lexus V6s is associated with the 1MZ-FE (3.0L, older ES300/RX300) and to a lesser extent the 2GR-FSE (direct injection IS/GS), not the port-injected 2GR-FE in the ES350
Year range 2007-2017 is overly broad; any 2GR-FE oil-related issues are concentrated in 2007-2009 production
Lexus's own position is that 1 quart per ~2,000 miles is within 'normal' factory tolerance, undermining the description's framing as a defect
evidence: Search results show the 2GR-FE's documented problems are timing cover FIPG oil leaks (2007-2009 ES350/RX350/Camry, largely resolved by 2010) and a VVT-i oil hose Limited Service Campaign for 2007-2008 ES350. Forum discussions explicitly note Lexus has no campaigns or TSBs for 2GR-FE internal oil consumption, and the piston-ring defect described in the entry actually matches the 2AZ-FE 4-cylinder or 1MZ-FE V6, not the 2GR-FE.

title: Carbon Buildup on Intake Valves (2.0T)
issues: The 8AR-FTS engine uses dual injection (D-4ST) with both direct AND port injection, which specifically sprays fuel over intake valves to prevent carbon buildup - directly contradicting the description's premise
Year range is wrong: the 2.0T IS200t/IS300 was offered 2016-2020, not through 2022 (IS300 2.0T was discontinued after 2020; 2021-2022 IS300 RWD uses the 3.5L V6 detuned, not the 2.0T)
Some sources note the 8AR-FTS can still experience some carbon buildup, but it is not a widely documented or common issue for this engine specifically due to its port injection capability

issues: Macan PDK is a WET-clutch dual-clutch transmission, not dry-clutch as described - this is a factual error about the mechanical design

Repair cost low-end ($300) is unrealistic; transfer case replacement typically runs $3000-5000+ and PDK service/replacement is far higher

title: Intermediate Shaft End-Play and Bearing Wear
issues: Entry frames 'intermediate shaft end-play' as a distinct diagnostic issue with a specific 0.10mm threshold; this specific measurement protocol is not a widely documented Porsche-recognized diagnostic — the well-known issue is IMS bearing failure itself

The 2006-2008 models have ~1% failure rates and require engine disassembly, making the cost estimate and uniform severity rating inaccurate.

Cost range may be low for full timing cover bolt repair (historically $9-12K engine-out, though engine-in procedures have reduced this)

The entry incorrectly merges these into one issue and misattributes the EA839 family to the entire 2015-2023 range.

title: Coolant Pipe and Fitting Leaks
issues: Description conflates the well-known 996/997 GT1-block glued coolant pipe failure with the 991's different leak pattern (O-ring/seal failures at thermostat housing and plastic pipe junctions, typically at the rear engine area, not 'near the front radiators')

title: Coolant Leak at Turbo Connections

Actual well-documented coolant issue is the coolant expansion/reservoir tank cracking at the seam (engine-out repair) and water pump failures

No TSB or forum evidence was found supporting the specific failure points described in the entry.

title: Coolant Pipe and Distribution Housing Leak
issues: Year range 2010-2020 is too broad; Porsche switched to bolted-on coolant pipes for the 2015 model year, so affected years are primarily 2010-2014 (lawsuit covers 2010-2016)

Repairs typically cost $2,500-$4,000 and the leak is hidden under the intake manifold, consistent with the entry, but the entry's year range, V6 inclusion, and described failure mechanism are inaccurate.

title: Coolant Leak at Turbo Connections
issues: The specific failure mode described (plastic turbo water line connections and coolant housings cracking from thermal cycling) is not a documented common issue for the 718 Cayman

Documented coolant-related issues on the 718 Cayman are primarily water pump failures (bearings/impeller) and changeover valve/vacuum leaks triggering cooling system faults, not turbo water line cracks

evidence: Forum and RepairPal sources document coolant leaks on the 718 Cayman primarily caused by water pump failures and changeover valve/vacuum line issues triggering cooling system faults, not by plastic turbo water line connections cracking from thermal cycling. No TSBs or widely-reported owner complaints match the specific failure mode described in the entry.

title: AC Compressor Failure and Clutch Burnout

title: Turbo Coolant Line Leak
issues: Description misidentifies the failure mode: the well-documented Cayenne coolant leak issue involves plastic coolant transfer pipes in the engine V valley and glued-in fittings on the thermostat housing/water distributor, NOT turbocharger coolant feed lines with crimped fittings and rubber sections

Repair cost range ($600-$1800) is low; real-world quotes commonly run $1500-$4000 due to intake manifold removal (and sometimes engine drop) required for access

evidence: Multiple independent sources (Rennlist, RennTech, 6SpeedOnline, ECS Tuning, Fluid MotorUnion, Dart Auto) confirm a widespread Cayenne V8 coolant leak issue, but it involves plastic coolant pipes/water distributor fittings under the intake manifold — not turbocharger coolant feed lines. Repair typically requires intake removal and frequently costs $2000-$4000, with some independent shops doing it cheaper.

title: Turbo Coolant Line Leak
issues: Misidentified component: actual failure is plastic coolant transfer/Y-pipe under intake manifold (PA66 nylon with aluminum fittings), not rubber turbo coolant feed lines

Labor-intensive access (intake manifold removal, or engine drop for rear distributor) makes typical repair costs higher than the listed $500-$1500 range.

title: Transfer Case Seal Leak
issues: The well-documented Macan transfer case issue is primarily internal clutch plate failure (addressed via gas nitrocarburizing of clutch plates and a 7-year extended warranty), not output shaft seal leaks as described

Owner reports do mention seal seepage at the transmission/transfer case interface, but the headline issue is internal clutch plate failure rather than output shaft seal leaks, and the affected year range is narrower than 2015-2023.

title: Cylinder Scoring on 981 GTS and GT4

Repair cost range cannot be verified for a system that doesn't exist on this vehicle

title: Water-Cooled Cylinder Scoring on 992 Generation
issues: Bore scoring is a documented issue for older M96/M97 engines (1997-2008) and to a lesser extent the 9A1 engine in 997.2/991.1, NOT the 992 generation
